Article Title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max get Variable Aperture as 'most important' camera feature: What it means for users
Article Text:
Apple iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max

Aperture is the part of a camera most phone users never see

The useful bit is what happens when you take control

It is not just about low light

The aperture is only on one camera

Apple is adding more control to video too

The idea isn't new to smartphones

The bigger camera change is the combination

What variable aperture actually changes for iPhone users

Apple has added variable aperture to the main camera on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. This will offer users a physical way to control how much light reaches the sensor for the first time on an iPhone.The feature sits alongside a new 48MP Fusion Main camera, a redesigned sensor and new Pro Controls. Apple says the six laser-cut blades inside the lens can move between four aperture settings, while the camera can also adjust the aperture automatically depending on the scene.That sounds like a minor hardware upgrade. But it is not. The lens opening affects exposure, depth of field, and how motion is captured, so giving the iPhone aperture control adds something software alone can't quite duplicate.Apple's description is straightforward: "iPhone 18 Pro has a new 48 megapixel fusion main camera with variable aperture for creative control that wasn't possible before," Apple said. "This is the most advanced camera we've ever made."Aperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. It is measured using f-numbers such as f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0.The lower the f-number, the wider the opening and the more light reaches the sensor.A wider aperture can therefore help in darker conditions. A narrower aperture lets in less light, but it also keeps more of the scene in focus.Most smartphone cameras use a fixed aperture. The lens has one opening, and the phone relies heavily on shutter speed, ISO, and computational photography to handle different lighting conditions.The iPhone 18 Pro changes that for its main camera. Its lens can open as wide as f/1.48 and then stop down to f/1.8, f/2.8 or f/4.0. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size.Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.The camera can make that decision automatically. In a darker scene, it can open the aperture to f/1.48 and let in more light. In brighter conditions, it can narrow the opening.For most people, the automatic system will do most of the work. The Camera app can choose an aperture based on the scene, just as it already decides on exposure and other settings.The difference is that iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max owners can also take control themselves.Apple's new Pro Controls let users manually change aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. A histogram can also be displayed to help judge exposure across a scene.That gives photographers another way to decide how a picture should look, instead of leaving every exposure decision to the camera.The most obvious example is depth of field. At a wider aperture such as f/1.48, the camera can produce more optical background blur when the subject is relatively close and the background is farther away.Stopping down to f/4.0 has the opposite effect. More of the scene can stay in focus, which can help with landscapes or group photos where people stand at different distances from the camera.That matters because a group shot can otherwise leave one person sharp while another, standing slightly farther away, falls outside the plane of focus. A narrower aperture gives the camera more room to keep those subjects in focus.It also gives photographers another option when deliberately introducing motion into an image. A narrower aperture reduces the amount of light entering the lens, making it easier to use a slower shutter speed when conditions are bright enough.The obvious benefit of opening the aperture is light. Apple says the main camera can open to ƒ/1.48 for low-light photography, letting more light reach the sensor.That can give the camera more flexibility before it has to compensate by increasing ISO or slowing the shutter speed. In practical terms, that can help preserve detail and reduce noise, while a fast enough shutter can keep moving subjects sharp.But variable aperture is useful in the opposite direction too.In bright daylight, photographers sometimes want a slower shutter speed to create motion blur. That can be useful with moving water, people, or cars, and it also matters in video, where shutter speed is normally tied to frame rate.A fixed wide aperture can make that difficult in strong sunlight because too much light reaches the sensor even when the shutter is already operating at its fastest useful setting. Stopping the lens down gives the camera another way to reduce exposure.There are limits, though. A range ending at f/4.0 does not eliminate the need for neutral-density filters in every bright-light situation. Photographers who want long exposures in direct sunlight may still need an ND filter to cut the light further.Apple's implementation has an important limitation. The variable aperture is on the main 24mm camera. It does not extend across the entire rear camera system.The ultra-wide and telephoto cameras don't have the same variable-aperture mechanism. That means the new optical control is available only when shooting through the main lens.This is also why the feature should not be viewed as a replacement for the other cameras or for computational photography. Exposure, autofocus, HDR, noise reduction and image processing still determine much of the final photograph.The hardware simply gives the camera another physical variable to work with before those processes take over.Aperture changes also feed into Apple's video features. The new Pro Controls work with video as well as photography, letting users manually adjust settings including aperture and shutter speed. That is especially relevant for people who want more predictable exposure rather than letting the phone change settings during recording.Apple has also added the ability to apply Cinematic effects after capture to videos recorded at up to 60 frames per second. That means users can make this adjustment after recording instead of committing to the effect while shooting.Time-lapse recording now supports 4K and Dolby Vision HDR, while Audio Mix has new algorithms designed to improve voice quality and isolate music.The combination is notable because Apple isn't presenting the variable aperture as an isolated camera specification. It is part of a broader attempt to give users more control over how photos and video are captured and processed.Apple is not the first phone maker to put a variable aperture in a smartphone. Samsung introduced a dual-aperture system with the Galaxy S9 series in 2018. That system switched between f/1.5 and f/2.4 depending on the lighting conditions.Huawei later introduced more flexible variable-aperture systems, while Xiaomi and Honor have also used the technology in flagship phones.The reason it has remained relatively uncommon is fairly simple: fitting a mechanical aperture mechanism into a smartphone camera adds complexity to an already tightly packed module.For years, phone makers instead concentrated on larger sensors, multiple cameras and computational photography. Those technologies can compensate for many of the limitations of a fixed aperture without adding moving parts to the lens.The iPhone 18 Pro's approach is therefore less about replacing computational photography than adding an optical control alongside it.The variable aperture gets most of the attention, but Apple has made several other changes to the camera system.The 48MP Fusion Main camera uses a new sensor and a new computational imaging pipeline that Apple says produces sharper, more detailed images. Photographic Styles now include additional texture and grain controls, giving users more ways to change the look of their photos.Apple has also added persistent subject tracking for photos and video, letting the camera keep following a person even if they temporarily disappear behind someone else in a crowd.Another feature aimed at photographers is Apple Reference Image. When Reference mode is used, the camera captures signed sensor data that Private Cloud Compute turns into what Apple describes as an "unalterable reference image." You can then view the reference alongside the main photograph in the Photos app.The idea is to compare the original sensor-derived reference with the photograph and identify whether changes have been made. Apple says the feature is intended to address image authenticity, particularly for photographers and photojournalists.Apple is also adding metadata support and upcoming support for the SynthID standard to help identify images generated or edited with AI.For someone who simply opens the Camera app and takes pictures, it may not change much. The phone can choose the aperture automatically, just as it already handles most exposure decisions. For people who shoot deliberately, the change is more useful.A wider f/1.48 setting can help in darker scenes. Stopping down can keep more of a group or landscape in focus. Manual aperture control can also be combined with shutter-speed control to create particular motion effects.It can even produce optical effects that fixed-aperture smartphone cameras cannot reproduce in the same way, including changes in how bright points of light appear at narrower apertures.But four aperture settings don't turn the iPhone into a dedicated interchangeable-lens camera. The sensor remains small compared with most conventional cameras, and the amount of natural optical background blur depends heavily on the distance between the camera, subject, and background.For many portraits, Apple's computational Portrait mode will still produce a stronger and more controllable background-blur effect.The same is true for long exposures in bright daylight. The f/1.48-to-f/4.0 range gives photographers more room, but it does not remove the physical limits imposed by available light.That is probably the right way to look at the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture. It gives the camera one more physical control over exposure and focus, while the sensor and software continue to determine what ultimately reaches the screen.For casual users, most of that will happen automatically. For photographers and videographers who want to decide how the shot is captured, the four aperture settings and Pro Controls make the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max considerably more flexible than a fixed-aperture iPhone.
Article Summary: Aperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size. Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.

Article Title: Google unveils five new sustainability initiatives in India
Article Text: Google is expanding its Solar API to cover more than 300 million rooftops in India, enabling faster and more accurate rooftop solar assessments. Installers can now evaluate a home’s solar potential without an on‑site visit, reducing time and cost. Platforms like Solar Ladder and OpenSolar have already integrated Solar API insights to streamline proposal creation and automate manual roof surveys.Google has signed a long‑term agreement with ReNew Power for a 150‑megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. The company will receive environmental attributes from the clean electricity generated, helping address electricity‑related emissions across its value chain. This marks Google’s second Scope 3‑focused solar project in India, bringing total added capacity to 300 MW.Google is partnering with Mitti Labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), a climate‑smart farming method that reduces methane emissions and conserves water. The initiative is expected to generate up to 3 million tonnes of CO₂e in near‑term warming impact (GWP20) and conserve billions of gallons of water.NASA‑enabled satellite verification will support monitoring and farmer adoption.The Google Center for Climate Technology has selected three inaugural projects focused on green workforce training and low‑carbon construction materials. Google is adding two new focus areas—water stewardship and waste & circularity—and is inviting proposals via the Manthan Platform. Selected applicants will receive support to develop scalable, data‑driven environmental solutions.Google has welcomed the first cohort of the DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet, featuring four Indian startups: Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests, and Climitra Carbon. These companies use AI, Geo‑AI, drones and satellite models to empower farmers, scale agroforestry, restore biodiversity, and convert biomass into biochar.These five initiatives reflect Google’s push to combine AI, research partnerships and local innovation to advance sustainable development and climate resilience across India.
Article Summary: Google has signed a long‑term agreement with ReNew Power for a 150‑megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. Google is partnering with Mitti Labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt a climate‑smart farming method. Google has welcomed the first cohort of the DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet.

Article Title: 1980s AI Photo trend: 5 ChatGPT prompts to create Kerala-style retro images

Add authentic 1980s hairstyles and simple traditional jewellery. Set the photograph inside a modest Kerala home with wooden furniture and subtle traditional decor.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: In 2023, a California materials scientist built a device that pulled drinking water from desert air; it produced 35 litres a day at just 20% humidity
Article Text:
AI Representation: A device collects drinking water from dry desert air and fills a reservoir with fresh water. Image credits: Chatgpt

The harvester ran on ambient sunlight alone

How the output shifted with humidity

An earlier MOF proved the concept could work at 20 percent humidity

Why dry air poses the harder engineering challenge

From a two-hand prototype toward household-scale units

In the summer of 2023, scientists from UC Berkeley took a machine that could be held by two hands to Death Valley National Park in North America, which is one of the most arid and hot locations on the continent and allowed it to operate using only the energy of the sun. It pulled water vapor out of the desert air, converted it to liquid and produced drinkable water without a battery, a plug, or any moving parts drawing outside power. The chemist behind the work, Omar Yaghi, had spent years building toward that single field test.This device uses a MOF, or metal-organic framework, an ultra-porous crystalline structure that Yaghi's team has studied for years. The specific MOF used here is MOF-303, an aluminum MOF that captures water molecules from the air at night, when humidity is usually higher in the desert and releases them during the day as sunlight warms the material. The resulting vapor condenses on a cooler surface within the device and flows into a container.Testing the same device in two very different climates allowed the team to isolate the effect of humidity.In Death Valley, the harvester achieved up to 210 grams of water per kilogram of MOF-303 per day in a single day-and-night cycle, marking the highest output the team recorded at that site. By comparison, in the milder, more humid air of Berkeley, the same device reached up to 285 grams per kilogram per day under similar passive operation, though Berkeley's daily averages ran lower on some days. The results appear in a 2023 paper in Nature Water , MOF water harvester produces water from Death Valley desert air in ambient sunlight, by Woochul Song, Zhiling Zheng, Ali Alawadhi and Yaghi, and they mark roughly double what an earlier passive version of the harvester had managed.Death Valley’s new technology is a further development of the tests done on the material by Yaghi and his team six years back, in collaboration with mechanical engineers from MIT. This project, which was done in 2017, involved a totally new material made up of zirconium and referred to as MOF-801. The results proved that even at low humidity levels between 20% and 30%, a solar-driven water harvester could generate significant quantities of water.The findings, published in Science as Water harvesting from air with metal-organic frameworks powered by natural sunlight, reported a yield of about 2.8 liters of water per kilogram of MOF per day at relative humidity as low as 20 percent, using only sunlight to drive the release step; some press accounts described the same result as roughly 2.8 liters over a 12-hour test window, though the paper itself reports it as a daily figure. The 2023 Nature Water study notes that switching from zirconium-based MOF-801, priced at $160 per kilogram, to aluminum-based MOF-303, priced at $3 per kilogram, made the harvester far cheaper to build; the higher water yield came from MOF-303's own adsorption behavior, not from its lower price.Water extraction from moist air is fairly easy since most dehumidifiers function on the principle of cooling air below its dew point. Nevertheless, air in the desert presents a different challenge. This is because at relative humidity less than 20%, the dew point may be below the freezing point, meaning that a lot of energy will be required for the process of condensation. MOFs are designed such that their pores are capable of adsorbing water molecules, even at very low levels of humidity, while heat can desorb them.The Death Valley test was, by design, a proof‑of‑concept prototype rather than a final, household‑scale product. The scientists pointed out that the tiny size and limited daily amount of water provided by the device were more appropriate for proving the concept behind the chemical reaction rather than for providing enough drinking water for a family's daily needs. Yaghi also disclosed in a public interview that further development along the same lines of MOF chemistry greatly enhanced production, and his firm began manufacturing more efficient devices capable of producing water in quantities of dozens or even hundreds of liters each day.
Article Summary: Device uses a MOF, or metal-organic framework, an ultra-porous crystalline structure that Yaghi's team has studied for years. The specific MOF used is MOF-303, an aluminum MOF that captures water molecules from the air at night and releases them during the day as sunlight warms the material. The resulting vapor condenses on a cooler surface within the device and flows into a container.

Article Title: In 1985, Andy Warhol created digital art on an Amiga computer; nearly 30 years later, researchers recovered 28 never-before-seen images from his floppy disks
Article Text:
Warhol used the Amiga to explore how his familiar artistic style could work in a new digital medium.

How the forgotten files were recovered

The recovered works show Warhol using digital tools to recreate subjects that were already strongly associated with his art.

Warhol’s experiments with a new medium

In 1985, Andy Warhol experimented with digital art on an Amiga computer as part of a commission from Commodore International. Nearly 30 years later, researchers recovered 28 previously unseen digital images created by the artist from floppy disks stored in the archives of The Andy Warhol Museum.The images had remained inaccessible because the files were saved in an obsolete format, according to The Andy Warhol Museum. Members of the Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) Computer Club worked with museum staff, artists and researchers to recover the data from the ageing floppy disks.Warhol, who earned a bachelor’s degree in fine arts from Carnegie Mellon University in 1949, used the Amiga to explore how his familiar artistic style could work in a new digital medium. The recovered works include experiments with Campbell’s soup cans, Botticelli’s Venus, Marilyn Monroe, a banana and portraits.The recovery project began after artist Cory Arcangel, who described himself as a "Warhol fanatic and lifelong computer nerd", learnt about Warhol’s Amiga experiments through a 1985 Commodore infomercial available on YouTube. His interest eventually led to a collaboration involving The Andy Warhol Museum, Carnegie Museum of Art, Carnegie Mellon University and the CMU Computer Club.Arcangel first approached The Andy Warhol Museum in 2011 about restoring the Amiga hardware held by the museum and checking whether files could still be recovered from its associated disks. He later worked with Tina Kukielski of the Carnegie Museum of Art, who helped connect the project with Golan Levin, a CMU art professor and director of the Frank-Ratchye STUDIO for Creative Inquiry.Levin connected Arcangel with the CMU Computer Club, a student group known for its work with obsolete computer hardware and "retrocomputing". The group found that even reading the old floppy disks could put their contents at risk. The recovery therefore required unusual equipment and methods.By February 2013, the Computer Club had prepared a plan for handling the fragile disks. Members then worked with Amber Morgan, collections manager at The Andy Warhol Museum, and other archivists to try to extract the data.At first, there was no certainty that Warhol’s artwork was still present on the disks. Many of the floppy disks were system and application disks. However, the researchers discovered that Warhol had also saved his own data on them.The directory listings provided the first major clue. Files with names such as "campbells.pic" and "marilyn1.pic" suggested that images might still exist. But the excitement quickly turned into a technical problem because the files were stored in a format that available utilities could not recognise.The Computer Club’s forensics experts eventually reverse-engineered the unknown format. This allowed them to access 28 digital images that had never been seen before. Experts at The Andy Warhol Museum judged the images to be in Warhol’s style. At least 11 of the recovered images also carried Warhol’s signature.The recovered works show Warhol using digital tools to recreate subjects that were already strongly associated with his art. Campbell’s soup cans, Venus and self-portraits appear among the images.Instead of traditional painting or printing methods, the works use digital processes available through the Amiga. These include pattern flood fills, palletised colour and copy-and-paste collage.The museum said Warhol’s Amiga experiments ranged from simple doodles and photographs of a desktop to digital versions of his familiar subjects. One work from the series, a portrait of Debbie Harry, was already part of The Warhol’s collection.Cory Arcangel said, "What's amazing is that by looking at these images, we can see how quickly Warhol seemed to intuit the essence of what it meant to express oneself.
Article Summary: Andy Warhol experimented with digital art on an Amiga computer in 1985. Nearly 30 years later, researchers recovered 28 previously unseen digital images created by the artist from floppy disks stored in the archives of The Andy Warhol Museum. The recovered works show Warhol using digital tools to recreate subjects that were already strongly associated with his art.

Article Title: China planted three types of forests on the Loess Plateau; 18 years later, natural forests held 8% more soil moisture
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Natural forests held 8% more soil moisture

How did natural forests improve soil water storage

Image AI generated

Why did natural forests retain more soil moisture

China’s long-running effort to restore the degraded Loess Plateau has revealed a difference between forests planted by people and those allowed to regenerate naturally. Researchers spent 18 years monitoring four forest types in the region, comparing plantations of Pinus tabuliformis, Platycladus orientalis and Robinia pseudoacacia with a natural secondary forest. The results showed that the natural forest had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests, while recording greater macroporosity and stronger water movement through the soil. Its soil held more water after rainfall, with average soil water storage reaching around 6 mm, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. Over the 2006–2024 monitoring period, the natural forest consistently maintained higher soil water content, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining moisture trends. The researchers also found that natural forest soils had lower bulk density and higher levels of soil organic carbon and total nitrogen.These differences suggest that allowing forests to recover naturally may improve the soil’s ability to absorb and retain rainfall. The findings could help guide restoration across water-limited landscapes, where choosing suitable forest types is important for balancing vegetation recovery with available water resources.According to the study published in Water Resources Research, titled ‘Natural Forests Accelerate Soil Hydrological Processes and Enhance Water-Holding Capacities Compared to Planted Forests After Long-Term Restoration ’, natural secondary forests had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests. They also had 68.7% greater macroporosity, a 13.7% larger mean equivalent pore diameter and 34.2% higher saturated hydraulic conductivity. The researchers also recorded higher soil organic carbon, field capacity and available water content in the natural forests.The difference was also visible across the 18-year monitoring period. Natural secondary forests consistently maintained higher soil water content, with peak values reaching 0.28 cm³ per cm³, particularly after substantial rainfall. Pinus tabuliformis showed a slight increase in soil moisture over the period, reaching 0.24 cm³ per cm³, while Robinia pseudoacacia and Platycladus orientalis showed declining soil moisture trends, with average values between 0.15 and 0.22 cm³ per cm³.The researchers found clear differences in soil structure between the forests. Natural secondary forest soils had the highest macroporosity and better-connected pores. Their mean macroporosity was 0.113 mm³ per mm³, compared with 0.089 for Robinia pseudoacacia, 0.065 for Platycladus orientalis and 0.047 for Pinus tabuliformis.The natural forests also showed faster soil-water processes during rainfall. Average soil water storage was around 6 mm in the secondary forests, compared with 3–4 mm in the planted forests. The researchers linked this greater storage to the natural forests’ higher macroporosity and pore connectivity, which allowed rainfall to be redistributed and infiltrate the soil more efficiently.Soil moisture in Pinus tabuliformis and Robinia pseudoacacia dropped substantially during the driest period from June to August. In the upper 60 cm of soil, moisture fell. Platycladus orientalis retained more water in deeper layers, but moisture still declined in the upper soil. The secondary forest maintained higher and more stable moisture, particularly in the upper 60 cm.The researchers also found that the secondary forest had lower bulk density, at about 1.0 g per cm³, in the three planted forests. Its soils also contained generally higher levels of total nitrogen and soil organic carbon. The study’s analysis identified soil properties such as bulk density and organic carbon, together with understory plant diversity, as important factors associated with soil hydrological processes and water-holding capacity.

The results showed that the natural forest had 8% higher soil moisture than the planted forests.

The story shows what happens when an island is given a chance to recover

For decades, introduced animals transformed some of New Zealand’s remote subantarctic islands, where native plants and wildlife had evolved without large grazing mammals or land predators. Sheep were among the animals introduced to islands where people attempted to establish farming, while cats arrived alongside human settlement and ships. Removing those introduced species eventually gave some island ecosystems a chance to recover. The Department of Conservation (DOC) describes the removal of introduced pests from New Zealand’s offshore islands as an important part of restoring ecosystems that had been heavily altered by animals brought there by people.New Zealand’s subantarctic islands are isolated landscapes with plant communities that developed without the grazing pressure created by introduced livestock. When people brought animals such as sheep to these islands, the consequences could be substantial. Grazing reduced vegetation and altered the structure of plant communities, while other introduced mammals could compound the damage by eating native plants or prey.DOC notes more broadly that New Zealand’s native forests and ecosystems were not adapted to mammalian browsers, meaning introduced ungulates can cause major changes in vegetation structure and composition.The contrast between islands with introduced mammals and those without them became especially useful for conservationists. DOC describes pest-free offshore islands as examples of what New Zealand ecosystems can look like when introduced mammals are absent. In these places, native vegetation can recover and populations of native birds and other wildlife can become far more abundant.That makes the removal of livestock more than simply the end of farming. It can become the beginning of ecological recovery.Once grazing animals are removed, vegetation no longer faces the same constant pressure from browsing and trampling. Plants that have been suppressed can regenerate, while seedlings and taller vegetation have a better chance of surviving.This experience with offshore islands has shown how dramatic this recovery can be. Conservation staff have described pest-free islands as places where the abundance and diversity of life can be strikingly different from nearby areas where introduced mammals remain. Forests became filled with continuous bird song after introduced cats were removed from Little Barrier Island, followed later by the successful eradication of rats.The same principle applies across New Zealand's offshore islands, removing the animals that are causing ecological damage allows natural processes to take over again.Sheep were not the only introduced mammals that changed these remote environments. Feral cats became serious predators on several New Zealand islands, where native birds had evolved without mammalian predators.Cats can be particularly damaging on islands because many native birds nest or feed on the ground and have few natural defences against introduced predators. DOC identifies introduced mammals, including feral cats, as major threats to native wildlife. On Little Barrier Island, for example, The cats had wiped out saddlebacks by the 1960s. The last cat there was removed in 1980, after which saddlebacks were returned to the island.The removal of cats also demonstrated how one conservation action can unlock another. Once the cats were gone, conservationists could begin restoring bird populations without exposing newly released animals to the same predator.New Zealand's offshore-island conservation work eventually moved from controlling individual pests to attempting complete eradication. DOC describes the eradication of introduced mammals from islands as an important conservation tool because isolated islands provide an opportunity to remove pests completely and then prevent them from returning.That approach has produced some of New Zealand's most dramatic restoration successes. Conservation specialists point to pest-free offshore islands as living demonstrations of what ecosystems can look like when introduced mammals are removed. Bird numbers can increase, vegetation can recover and species that disappeared from an island can sometimes be returned.The transformation is particularly striking because the islands themselves have not been rebuilt. Once the introduced pressures are removed, much of the recovery comes from the ecosystem's own ability to regenerate.New Zealand's offshore islands have become some of the country's most important conservation laboratories precisely because their isolation makes it possible to remove invasive mammals and protect the results. This work has shown that an island that once appeared permanently altered can change substantially once grazing animals and predators are removed.The lesson extends beyond any single island. Introduced sheep could reshape vegetation through grazing, while cats and other predators could suppress native wildlife. Removing those pressures did not simply make the islands quieter, it allowed native ecosystems to begin functioning more like they had before the arrival of introduced mammals.For New Zealand's conservationists, pest-free islands offer a glimpse of what restoration can achieve, remove the animals that do not belong, protect the survivors, and allow the vegetation and wildlife to rebuild themselves.

Article Title: In the 1970s, Washington tied thousands of discarded tyres together across 20 Puget Sound reefs to improve bottom fishing; decades later, the ropes failed and more than 100,000 tyres remained underwat
Article Text:

AI REPRESENTATION: Discarded vehicle tyres rest on the seafloor of Puget Sound, where they were once used to create artificial reefs for recreational fishing | ChatGPT

The reefs were built for bottom fishing

A reef material became a cleanup problem

A harbor seal along the coast of the Puget Sound | Wikimedia Commons

More than 100,000 tires are still being dealt with

Washington's experiment with artificial reefs in Puget Sound began with the practical goal of creating more structure on the seafloor for rockfish, lingcod and other bottom-dwelling fish while expanding recreational fishing opportunities. Discarded vehicle tires, among other materials, were bundled together and lowered into the water at 20 reef sites during the 1970s.A 2025 article from the University of Washington's School of Marine and Environmental Affairs describes the tire reefs as one of Puget Sound's clearest examples of how artificial habitat can produce unintended problems. The tires were tied together with polypropylene rope, and thousands were placed at each of the 20 sites.The University of Washington account says new federal laws and court decisions in the 1970s and 1980s tightened restrictions on salmon fishing, which prompted recreational anglers to put more attention on bottom fishing for species such as rockfish and lingcod. Washington's Department of Fish and Wildlife worked with recreational fishing groups as artificial reef construction expanded. Tires were only one of several materials used, while other reefs incorporated concrete, natural rock, plastics, PVC, vessels, barges and even train cars.The basic idea was to add vertical relief and structural complexity to parts of the seabed that provided relatively little cover.Natural rocky reefs provide crevices and surfaces where algae and invertebrates can live, while smaller fish can use the structure for shelter from predators and currents. The polypropylene rope deteriorated, which allowed individual tires and sections of the artificial structures to move away from their original locations. The tires became loose objects on the seafloor and, in some locations, eventually reached shorelines, instead of remaining as stable reef units. The Washington Department of Natural Resources now considers the old tire structures an environmental problem rather than a successful fish habitat, and its Tire Pile Removal Program says thousands of surplus automotive tires were placed on the bottom of Puget Sound during the 1970s and 1980s to attract native reef fish and improve recreational fishing. The agency says the artificial structures have since been judged unsuccessful and has begun planning and carrying out their removal.DNR began prioritizing removal work in 2019 and has worked with the Washington Department of Ecology, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission and Washington Scuba Alliance to locate and survey the old reefs. DNR's survey work between 2019 and 2021 examined 20 locations using multibeam sonar and underwater video. Tires were found at 14 of those sites, with major differences between locations in the number of tires and the size of the affected areas.The University of Washington report says that the material has weathered and fragmented, while chemical compounds associated with degraded tires can enter the surrounding environment. It also notes that tire surfaces did not provide the same biological communities found on more suitable artificial reef materials.A March 2025 KING 5 report estimated that more than 100,000 tires remained in Puget Sound from the old reef program, while noting that the exact number is uncertain because not all tire placements are mapped. DNR has identified multiple priority sites, and its work involves locating tire piles, recovering them from the water and sending the damaged material for appropriate disposal.The original reefs were intended to solve a fisheries problem by adding structure to the seabed, and decades later, the same structures have become objects that marine managers are trying to remove. The contrast has also shaped how newer artificial reefs in Puget Sound are designed, with greater attention to durable materials, site selection and long-term maintenance.

The tires were tied together with polypropylene rope, and thousands were placed at each of the 20 sites. Washington's experiment with artificial reefs in Puget Sound began with the practical goal of creating more structure on the seafloor for rockfish, lingcod and other bottom-dwelling fish.

Article Title: Palo Alto built San Francisco Bay’s first horizontal levee to reuse treated wastewater; the 500-foot living slope restores marsh habitat and tests defenses against sea-level rise
Article Text:
Palo Alto’s 500-foot living levee reuses treated wastewater to restore marsh habitat and fight seas (Image Credit: City of Palo Alto)

What is a horizontal levee?

Turning treated wastewater into a resource

Restoring a missing habitat zone

A test for future Bay Area defences

A shoreline defence can be more than a wall. In Palo Alto, California, engineers have built a broad, gently sloping landscape designed to protect the coast while functioning like a living ecosystem. The project sits along Harbor Marsh in the Palo Alto Baylands and combines native vegetation, treated wastewater and a nature-based approach to sea-level rise. Unlike a conventional concrete or steep-sided levee, the new structure is designed to provide habitat as well as help reduce the effects of waves and rising water.According to the City of Palo Alto, the completed project is a 500-foot-long horizontal levee and the first of its kind on the San Francisco Bay shoreline to use treated wastewater from the city's Regional Water Quality Control Plant to irrigate native plantings. The project was completed in September 2026 after construction began in 2025.A traditional levee typically creates a relatively steep barrier between a community and the water. A horizontal levee takes a different approach. Instead of relying primarily on a hard wall, it uses a wide, gradual slope planted with vegetation. The Palo Alto project is intended to create a transition between upland areas and the existing tidal marsh.Its vegetation includes freshwater marsh, wet meadow, riparian scrub and other native habitat types. As sea levels rise, this broad transition zone can give marsh vegetation space to move gradually uphill rather than ending abruptly at a fixed barrier. The design is therefore intended to serve several purposes at once: improve habitat, help the shoreline adapt to rising seas, reduce wave impacts and provide a way to further treat already-treated wastewater.One of the project's most unusual features is its use of treated wastewater. Palo Alto's Regional Water Quality Control Plant produces highly treated wastewater. Instead of allowing all of that water to serve only as a conventional discharge, the horizontal levee uses it underground to irrigate plants growing on the slope.According to the City of Palo Alto, this water is replacing freshwater that historically reached the Baylands through local creeks but was later reduced or cut off because of flood-control channelisation and urban development. As the treated water moves through the soil beneath the planted slope, the system can also provide additional "polishing" treatment before the water reaches the Bay. This creates a circular approach in which water that has already undergone treatment becomes part of a habitat-restoration and climate-adaptation project.The levee is also intended to restore a type of habitat that has become increasingly rare around the San Francisco Bay shoreline. The area between freshwater and tidal salt marsh can support a variety of plants and provide important transitional habitat for wildlife. Palo Alto's project is designed to restore these conditions around Harbor Marsh, potentially benefiting species that use the surrounding wetlands, including the endangered Ridgway's rail and salt marsh harvest mouse.The project is not simply about planting vegetation. Researchers will monitor how the soil develops, how plants establish themselves and how the ecosystem changes over time. The goal is to determine whether the living slope can continue functioning as sea levels rise.The word "pilot" is important to the project. Palo Alto is treating the 500-foot structure as a real-world experiment that can provide data for future shoreline projects. Scientists and agencies, including the U.S. Geological Survey, University of California Davis, California State University Channel Islands and the San Francisco Estuary Partnership, are involved in studying its performance. They will examine vegetation, soil accumulation, ecosystem complexity and habitat suitability. The idea is that lessons from this relatively small project could eventually influence larger shoreline-defence schemes around the Bay.Palo Alto's approach reflects a broader shift in thinking about coastal protection. As sea levels rise, communities increasingly have to protect infrastructure without sacrificing the ecosystems that surround it. The horizontal levee attempts to address both challenges simultaneously: instead of separating the city from nature with a hard barrier, it uses a planted landscape to make the shoreline more resilient. If the pilot performs as intended, this 500-foot stretch of living shoreline could become a model for how other Bay Area communities approach the difficult task of preparing for a higher sea.
Article Summary: Palo Alto's 500-foot-long horizontal levee is the first of its kind on the San Francisco Bay shoreline to use treated wastewater to irrigate native plantings. The project was completed in September 2026 after construction began in 2025. Researchers will monitor how the soil develops, how plants establish themselves and how the ecosystem changes over time.

Article Title: Meet Henry Xie: The 17-year-old Portland student whose method made smaller AI models more empathetic in at least 90% of tests
Article Text:
Henry Xie

A two-step framework for teaching empathy

Making human-focused AI available on personal devices

A 17-year-old student from Portland, Oregon, has developed a two-step training method that helps small artificial intelligence models copy the empathetic communication style of much larger systems. The method achieved higher empathy ratings in at least 90 per cent of comparison tests. Henry Xie, a senior at Westview High School in Portland, created the computer science project "Distilling Empathy From Large Language Models" for the Regeneron Science Talent Search, the leading science and mathematics competition for high school seniors in the United States. Official information published by the Society for Science confirmed that Xie was named a national finalist and received a $25,000 award for his research into ethical artificial intelligence. Xie's method tackles a key problem in current AI technology. Large language models (LLMs) with billions of parameters, such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, can produce detailed and emotionally supportive responses. However, they need large amounts of computing power, costly server systems and a constant internet connection. Small language models (SLMs), on the other hand, can run directly on devices such as smartphones, laptops and wearable technology.They do not need the same level of server support and can respond with low delay. However, these smaller models have traditionally struggled to understand emotional details and often produce mechanical or detached replies.To close this gap, Xie created a two-step training framework that transfers empathetic reasoning from large AI systems to smaller models without increasing their memory or processing requirements. During the first training stage, Xie collected published examples of empathetic conversations produced by LLMs such as ChatGPT and Gemini. He based the data on established psychological ideas about communication and supportive listening. He then used these examples to train small language models and teach them basic patterns for using empathetic language. In the second stage, Xie added specific prompts that encouraged the smaller models to assess their own possible responses. By comparing stronger empathetic answers with weaker or dismissive ones, the models learned to choose responses that better recognised and responded to people's emotional states. Evaluation results published by the Society for Science show that when the responses were assessed using LLMs, the small models trained with Xie's method were rated as more empathetic than basic, untrained SLMs in at least 90 per cent of test situations.Alongside his research, Xie has also worked on technology access and AI ethics in his local community. The son of Fei Xie and Huaiyu Liu, he is president of the computer science club and captain of the varsity swim team at Westview High School. Xie is also a three-time semifinalist in the CyberPatriot National Youth Cyber Defense Competition, one of the main youth cybersecurity competitions in the United States, according to background information. Xie also co-founded Youth for Empathetic AI, a student-led non-profit group that connects high school researchers with academic mentors. The organisation aims to encourage the development of human-focused artificial intelligence and greater involvement by young people in discussions about AI governance."Corals in Hawaii grow so, so slowly that it may take hundreds of years to recover from an event like that," noted researchers in related computer science literature examining ethical models, emphasizing that foundational training approaches determine long-term AI behavior. By helping small language models produce empathetic responses directly on personal devices, Xie's research shows that advanced conversational features could work locally without sending sensitive user information to cloud servers. The findings could provide a way to add more emotionally aware AI features to everyday mobile apps, wellness tools and accessible consumer devices.
Article Summary: Henry Xie, a 17-year-old student from Portland, Oregon, developed a two-step training method that helps small artificial intelligence models copy the empathetic communication style of much larger systems. The method achieved higher empathy ratings in at least 90 per cent of comparison tests. Xie was named a national finalist and received a $25,000 award for his research into ethical artificial intelligence.

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: Glance brings agentic shopping to iOS
Article Text:

Bengaluru:

InMobi’s lock-screen unicorn Glance has launched its agentic shopping experience natively on iOS, integrating with Siri AI to enable users to seek shopping assistance through voice commands, as the company looks to shift shopping from apps to AI agents. Glance has clocked around $300 million in revenue.The platform combines Apple Intelligence with Glance’s three-layered technology stack and understanding of users’ past preferences and context to explain why a product may be relevant to them. It is an agent-to-agent integration with Siri rather than a lock-screen integration.Users upgrading to iOS 27 will be able to access Glance intelligence through Siri.For instance, users can photograph an apparel item and ask Siri where it can be bought. The Glance Agent can identify the product, surface relevant options and enable a virtual try-on experience.Glance has integrated Apple’s on-device models with its commerce intelligence. Its iOS experience uses Foundation Models and Core AI to enable on-device virtual try-ons, including image generation directly on the iPhone. The feature is currently experimental and is being developed with a focus on privacy.“This is a very deep-tech collaboration. Our investment is more on how we co-build this agentic commerce experience on Apple Intelligence,” said Mansi Jain, COO at Glance. The investment has primarily been in people and technology, with Glance’s technology team working closely with Apple’s developer team.Jain said the partnership was significant for Glance’s global positioning. “We are the only platform which is building from India for the world which is showcased at the Apple stage,” she said.Glance currently has 10 million monthly active users in the US and said around 15% of users are transacting through its agent. The company has not disclosed GMV.Glance expects more than 50.0% of consumers to shop through agents over the next two to three years. Jain said the Apple integration validates the company’s thesis that consumers will increasingly use agents for shopping.The company expects iOS users to have higher transaction values, with Jain saying industry ARPU (average revenue per user) for iOS users is typically about twice that of Android users.
Article Summary: InMobi’s lock-screen unicorn Glance has launched its agentic shopping experience natively on iOS. Users upgrading to iOS 27 will be able to access Glance intelligence through Siri. Glance expects more than 50.0% of consumers to shop through agents over the next two to three years.

Article Title: Dire straits: Brand on the run as Trump suggests Hormuz can be renamed in his honor
Article Text:
Trump’s latest push to rename the Strait of Hormuz adds another chapter to his growing campaign of political branding and geographic renaming

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Donald Trump has rescued a canal, invaded a country, conquered a gulf, annexed a lake -- at least on American maps -- and put his name on a performing-arts center. He now appears to have set his sights on the hottest waterway on the planet.The MAGA boss suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” -- because if you cannot solve a problem, you can at least rename it.The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal purposes. Last week he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, saying the US had been treated badly by Canada. He then helpfully suggested that the Atlantic or Pacific could be next, saying, “We have a gulf and we have a lake…Now all we need is an ocean. ”The President, someone jibed, appears to be collecting bodies of water like refrigerator magnets.The joke became even better when Google Maps and Apple Maps fell in line.Google changed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users over the weekend. Apple followed on Tuesday. Canadians, however, continue to see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere may see both names. In other words, the lake has acquired the geographic equivalent of dual citizenship.The tech companies' compliance prompted criticism from illuminati who argue that private corporations should not allow political pressure to dictate historical and geographic nomenclature. MapQuest, an internet relic many Americans had forgotten existed, refused to make the change and suddenly discovered the most effective marketing strategy in Silicon Valley: stand up to Trump. Its downloads reportedly surged, giving it the kind reception normally reserved for rock bands that haven’t toured for a long time or sports legends making a comeback.There is also an awkward business joke buried underneath all this. Trump built his political persona partly on branding himself as a master businessman, but his corporate record includes repeated failures and bankruptcies in hotels and casinos; His casino empire alone went through multiple Chapter 11 restructurings. Trump-branded ventures have also included products and licensing deals that did not last.Late-night television has naturally treated Trump's naming obsession as premium material. The Atlantic, meanwhile, took the joke to its logical conclusion in a satirical vision of a future America in which everything is renamed “America” or “Trump,” leaving citizens unable to distinguish between brands of products, goods, and structures.Political analysts however see a serious calculation behind what many consider trolling. The renaming campaign sure is presidential theater -- cheap to stage, impossible for the internet and tv to resist, and almost guaranteed to ignite social media. But it also serves to distract people from more pressing issues -- such as cost of living and democracy going down the tubes.
Article Summary: Trump suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf Of America for US federal purposes.

Article Title: Sam Altman to everyone saying China will beat US after he agreed with Dario Amodei's view that AI could kill all of us; says: We do not mean stopping, but that it should ...
Article Text:
Sam Altman

Read OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s complete post here

The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence.

Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools.

For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes.

We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.
Article Summary: The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, says OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot, he says.
